Do correct answers have stable latent knowledge support?

A correct answer is an observable outcome. This study asks whether its internal knowledge support stays stable when the elicitation condition changes.

Shi Chuancheng·Li Shangze·Wu Wenhua·Hu Kun·Shen Fei·Wang Zhiyong·Chua Tat-Seng

October 11, 2026 ·Preprint ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

Correct outputs can coexist with substantially different levels of internal stability. LSS and KTS measure the stability of individual knowledge states and their relational structure, with LatentDPO exploring an editing application.

4,411Knowledge items
76,766Controlled queries
16Language models

Why this matters

Output accuracy alone cannot determine whether an answer rests on stable representations. Controlled changes in how knowledge is elicited provide a way to examine the support behind the answer.

How it works

  1. Average representations within each elicitation condition and correct shared shifts relative to a baseline.
  2. Use LSS for normalized state displacement and KTS for cross-condition consistency of pairwise distances.
  3. Evaluate controlled queries in EpiStableBench and use stability-aware preferences in LatentDPO.

What the study finds

EpiStableBench includes 4,411 items and 76,766 controlled queries. Across 16 LLMs, higher within-model stability generally accompanies better held-out accuracy, while larger or more accurate models are not consistently more stable. LatentDPO improves editing success and generalization in the evaluated integrations.

What this means

Knowledge stability adds an internal evaluation dimension beyond observed correctness; it complements accuracy rather than replacing it.
